title: A practice-session API
summary: Create routes for reading and adding practice entries in Express.
explanation: An API is an agreed way for programs to ask another program to do something. An HTTP request includes a method, a path, and sometimes a body of data. A route matches a method and path. GET /entries reads records; POST /entries asks to create one. A response has a status number and a body. JSON is a text format used to send objects and arrays between programs.

Number.isInteger requires a whole finite number, so it rejects a fraction, undefined, NaN, Infinity, and quoted numeric text. The bounds include 1 and 180; 0 and 181 fail. || means any invalid condition rejects the request. The default body = {} handles an omitted argument in this example. [...visits] makes a new array for the response, and push appends the valid record only after validation.

app.use installs middleware, code that runs before route handlers. express.json reads JSON request bodies, with a 20-kilobyte size limit. res.status chooses the status and res.json sends JSON. crypto.randomUUID creates a unique record identifier in this Node environment. A 200 means the read succeeded; 201 means a record was created; 400 asks the caller to fix invalid input; 404 means no matching route here. JSON parsing and other server failures are additional cases beyond this small route exercise.

For the exercise, implement handleRequest for /entries, validate before push, preserve saved records for later GET calls, and return 404 for /missing. The array is memory-only and disappears when the server stops. The browser checks your decision function; it does not launch Node or prove actual HTTP behavior. Download the supplied server and tests, install its declared packages locally, start it in one terminal, and run npm test in another to check the real routes.

title: A durable practice API
summary: Connect the API to a practice database and save entries.
explanation: Durable storage keeps data after a process stops. A JavaScript array is in memory and disappears on restart. A SQLite database opened with a file name stores records on disk. An adapter gives your code small methods such as save and load so callers can ask for storage without depending on its internal details. An adapter can be memory-only or durable; the method names alone do not prove persistence.

A prepared statement separates fixed SQL structure from the values supplied later. Placeholders such as ? stand for values, in order. The database handles their representation so a string value is not interpreted as extra SQL commands. Do not construct a query by concatenating untrusted input into its SQL text. Prepared statements address SQL input handling; range validation and ownership checks are still separate responsibilities.

For the browser exercise, saveEntry must call store.save and loadEntries must call store.load. The supplied a and b rows must survive a later c addition. The browser adapter makes copied rows but does not write a disk file. The downloaded server uses practice.sqlite and prepared statements with the same storage idea. Save a record, stop and restart that local server in the same folder, and read it again; only that actual restart test establishes its durability.

title: A protected practice API
summary: Add request validation, authorization, middleware, and failure handling.
explanation: Authentication asks who is signed in. Authorization asks whether that person may act on a particular record. Validation asks whether the proposed values are acceptable. A protected update needs all three. Being signed in does not grant access to someone else's record, and owning a record does not make an invalid duration acceptable.

The order makes the write safe. Return before assignment whenever a requirement fails. A request body can claim ownerId: 'nora', but anyone can submit that text. The trusted identity must come from a server-verified session, then be compared with the record's stored owner. The permission helper accepts that verified result; it must not be treated as proof that an arbitrary supplied object really represents a signed-in person.

A session is a server-recognized sign-in state. In a real flow, the server verifies credentials, issues an unpredictable token, and checks that token and its expiry on later requests. A cookie can carry the token. The browser's claim to be a user is not trusted without that verification. Middleware runs before the route, validates the session, and attaches a trusted identity such as req.user; the route then performs record-specific authorization.

For the exercise, authorizeUpdate receives verified-session fixtures and mutates entry.minutes only after all checks pass. Null session returns 401; mismatched ownership returns 403; invalid minutes returns 400; a valid owner update returns 200 with entry. True AND false AND true is false: valid sign-in and input cannot overcome failed ownership. To finish actual protection locally, connect real session verification before using this helper; the next full-stack project supplies a localhost sign-in flow.

import sqlite3, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    backup_path = Path(folder) / "backup.sqlite"
    source = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    source.executescript("CREATE TABLE notes(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,title TEXT); INSERT INTO notes VALUES(1,'Moon'),(2,'Ocean');")
    source.commit()
    with sqlite3.connect(backup_path) as saved:
        source.backup(saved)
    source.close()
    with sqlite3.connect(backup_path) as restored:
        assert restored.execute("PRAGMA integrity_check").fetchone()[0] == "ok"
        assert restored.execute("SELECT id,title FROM notes ORDER BY id").fetchall() == [(1,"Moon"),(2,"Ocean")]
    print("Disposable backup reopened and verified")

title: A reproducible project
summary: Declare dependencies and write instructions for running the project.
explanation: A reproducible project can be started from a clean copy using written instructions. A dependency is a package the code uses. package.json describes the project, needed packages, and runnable scripts. A lockfile, usually package-lock.json for npm, records the exact resolved package versions. Those are different jobs: a version range allows choices; the lockfile records the choices actually made.

Create main.js in the same disposable repro-demo folder with console.log('Clean start works');. Use these commands from the folder:
```bash
node --version
npm install
npm start
npm ci
npm start
```
The version check reports your runtime. install reads the manifest and creates or updates the lockfile when needed. start prints Clean start works. Once a matching lockfile exists, ci performs a clean installation using its recorded dependency versions, then the second start should work too. ci replaces node_modules, so use a clean practice copy for this walkthrough.

npm install and npm ci are not interchangeable in every situation. ci needs an existing lockfile that agrees with package.json; it fails instead of silently changing an inconsistent lockfile. Keep the manifest and lockfile in project history. node_modules contains installed package files and can usually be recreated. A lockfile improves consistency but does not promise identical behavior across every operating system or runtime version.

A README should tell another person the runtime requirement, setup command, launch command, and expected behavior. Here is plain example content, not a program:
```text
Repro demo
Requires Node.js 22.13 or newer.
Initial setup: npm install
Keep the generated package-lock.json.
Clean-copy setup with that lockfile: npm ci
Launch: npm start
Expected output: Clean start works
Third-party runtime dependencies: none
```
Test these instructions on a fresh copy so missing steps become visible. A screenshot of a successful run cannot replace the saved dependency information.

After the declaration passes, download the supplied files and follow the README locally. Confirm both the initial install and a clean-copy install with its saved lockfile, then start the program. The browser checks the declaration, not package installation. Read scripts before running someone else's project, and declare only packages it actually needs; invented dependencies create extra setup and review work without helping this program.

title: A tested feature
summary: Check normal, empty, boundary, failure, and concurrency cases where applicable.
explanation: A useful test checks promised behavior by comparing actual and expected results. It should fail when that behavior breaks. For clamping, a valid number below the range becomes the lower limit, one above becomes the upper limit, and one already inside stays unchanged. First reject the wrong kind of input; then apply the boundaries.

Run the test locally with Node installed:
```bash
node --test test-level.mjs
```
Passing assertions produce a passing test report. The module's demonstration console logs may also appear because importing evaluates that module. Temporarily replace the clamp with return value and rerun: outside-range assertions should fail. Restore the working code afterward. A test that only confirms the function exists would not catch that broken behavior.

Choose cases from the feature's requirements. Normal input verifies ordinary use; boundaries verify the exact included endpoints; just-outside values verify the transition; invalid input verifies rejection. Empty input can mean undefined here rather than a zero-length list. Concurrency tests are useful for shared balance updates, but this pure calculation has no shared mutable state, so concurrency is not a relevant risk for it.

For clampScore, use the exercise's 0-through-100 limits and preserve null for non-integers. Check 42, 0, 100, -5, and 110, plus undefined, NaN, Infinity, and 2.5. The inside result 100 and the just-outside result for 101 are both 100, but for different reasons: the first is already valid; the second must be clamped. Together they test the boundary transition.

The browser checks your function's behavior. Download score.mjs and test.mjs, replace the supplied score stub with your implementation, and run node --test test.mjs from their folder. A working browser function does not automatically edit that local stub. Break a relevant behavior briefly and confirm the local test fails, then restore and rerun. Passing tests are evidence for their stated cases, not proof of every possible property.

title: Build a reusable converter
summary: Write small functions that convert values with a supplied factor.
explanation: A function packages a named job so you can repeat it with different input. Parameters are the named input slots in its definition. Arguments are the actual values you pass when calling it. The return value is the result the call gives back. A conversion function can accept a distance and a conversion factor, multiply them, and return a new distance. Calling it twice does not require copying its calculation twice. It does not automatically choose units or a factor; the caller supplies the values with the intended meaning.

Swift can use an outside argument label and an inside parameter name. In _ length: Double, the underscore suppresses the outside label, so the first argument is written simply as 3. In factor: Double, factor is both the outside label and inside name. The caller writes factor: 0.5. Labels help a call communicate each input's purpose. Parentheses surround inputs, and a comma separates them. Putting the right number in the wrong position can change an answer even if the types still match, so read the call as well as the formula.

```swift
print(abs(-0.25))
print(abs(0.25))
```
Both print 0.25. abs receives a numeric value and returns its magnitude; it does not modify the supplied value. That is why abs(actual - expected) measures an unsigned difference.

A function's promised return type applies to all paths. This one has a single expression, length * factor, so Swift can also infer its return without the return word in a single-expression function body. The explicit version is useful while learning because the result's job is visible. Returning a number differs from printing it: a return allows later calculations, while print writes output. A function can do both, but the conversion exercise needs a returned Double so the checks and stored results can use it.

This second complete program reuses a function result in another calculation.

```swift
func cupsNeeded(_ batches: Double, cupsPerBatch: Double) -> Double {
    batches * cupsPerBatch
}
let cups = cupsNeeded(4, cupsPerBatch: 3)
let extraCups = cups + 1
print(cups)
print(extraCups)
```

Four batches times three cups per batch gives 12 cups. Adding one spare cup gives 13. This uses Swift's single-expression return for cupsNeeded. The numeric literals are accepted as Double inputs here because the function requires that type. Units are part of the meaning you give the numbers, not separate automatic labels in Double.

Multiplication applies a supplied rate or factor. Three cups per batch × four batches = twelve cups, because you need three for each of four groups. For distance using 1.6 kilometers per mile, two miles gives 3.2 kilometers and five gives 8. Floating-point values such as Double can approximate some decimal fractions, so compare an expected decimal using a small tolerance when appropriate. abs(actual - expected) measures how far apart they are without keeping a negative sign. It is different from rounding an incorrect answer until it looks right.

For the converter, define convert(_ value: Double, factor: Double) -> Double and return value times factor. Store shortTrip from convert(2, factor: 1.6) and longTrip from convert(5, factor: 1.6). The checks expect 3.2 and 8, including the stored names. The function should also work with other reasonable input values because the parameters drive its calculation. Explain what value, factor, and -> Double mean before the exercise, then predict a new call using the same multiplication.

title: Load data with cancellation
summary: Use an actor for shared entries and a cancellable task so older results cannot replace newer ones.
explanation: Asynchronous work can pause while waiting and resume later. async marks a Swift function that may suspend. await marks a call where your code can suspend while that work completes. Suspension lets other work make progress; it does not promise a particular thread or completion order. If one request starts first but takes longer, it may finish after a newer request. A loader therefore needs a deliberate policy: only the still-current request may change the visible result. Merely adding a longer delay cannot establish that policy.

Assign every request an increasing number. Increase requestID when starting new work and capture its value in a constant such as thisRequest. A helper accepts(request:current:) should return request == current, a Bool asking whether that request is still the latest one. If request 8 starts, then request 9 starts, only 9 remains current. If 9 finishes first, its result may be displayed; the late 8 result must be ignored. Cancellation alone is not enough because a task could finish before noticing the signal. Check both cancellation and the request ID after every await before updating protected data. In a guard with comma-separated conditions, every condition must succeed. !Task.isCancelled means cancellation has not been requested. += 1 increases the ID by one. In the supplied delay expression, condition ? first : second chooses one of two values, so request 1 gets the slower delay.

An actor protects its stored state through isolation: outside code must use its allowed access paths rather than changing the storage freely. actor PracticeStore can own its entries and accepted request number. Calls across the actor boundary use await because access may require waiting for that actor. Within its replacement method, guard request >= requestID else { return } rejects a response older than the last one stored. >= means greater than or equal to. That comparison accepts a newer replacement or a repeat of the same request. The loader's stricter equality check establishes which request is current; the store's number check separately prevents an old replacement from overwriting newer stored data.

@MainActor isolates the loader's state and methods to the main actor, the executor normally used for UI work. It does not make every operation inside an async method run without interruption. While an await suspends a method, other actor work may run and change its state. That is why a guard before await store.replace is not a substitute for another guard after it. private(set) allows reading a property outside its setting scope while keeping updates controlled. A method cancel should signal the task, increase requestID so old work is stale, and set an understandable message. It should preserve existing useful results unless the design deliberately says otherwise.

Model the loader's states in ordinary words: Ready before a request, Loading during it, Loaded with entries after success, Could not load after failure, or Load cancelled after cancellation. An outdated task should not change either the result or the current message. catch is CancellationError recognizes that error type; a following catch handles other errors. if accepts(...) inside those catches prevents a stale task from replacing a newer message. The supplied driver uses MainActor.run to read or construct main-actor state from its async context. It also stores two values in a tuple, accessed as .0 and .1, to inspect the result and message together.

```swift
let label = await MainActor.run { "Ready" }
print(label)
```
In a top-level async program this prints Ready. MainActor.run receives a synchronous closure, executes it on the main actor and returns its value through the awaited call. It does not make an entire async operation uninterrupted.

For the exercise, use the supplied real async driver: slow request 1 followed by faster request 2 should leave session-2 in both the loader and actor store. Request 0 should produce Could not load practice data. Explicit cancellation of request 1 should preserve session-2 and show Load cancelled. Store and cancel the Task, capture each new ID, and guard after awaits; do not depend on delays alone. In the math scenario, request A with ID 4 remains stale once B with ID 5 is current, so B stays visible even if A finishes last. The browser cannot execute this Swift concurrency or prove its scheduling behavior.

title: Save a durable practice log
summary: Separate the practice model from storage, save entries as JSON, and recover safely from bad data.
explanation: Persistence means keeping information outside the running program so it can be loaded later. A variable in memory normally disappears when the process ends. A file can remain on disk, but only if you write it to an appropriate location and keep that file. Separate the model, which describes an entry's information, from storage functions, which encode, write, read, and decode it. The screen can then use the result without being responsible for every file operation. This separation also makes success and recovery easier to inspect.

Codable combines Encodable and Decodable. Swift can generate their behavior for a struct whose stored properties also support them. JSONEncoder().encode(original) constructs an encoder and asks it to turn the array into Data. JSONDecoder().decode([ReadingEntry].self, from: bytes) names the exact expected type and converts bytes back. .self here refers to the type itself as an argument; it is not an array instance. The brackets in [ReadingEntry] mean an array of that model. If the bytes have a different shape or wrong field types, decoding can throw rather than producing valid entries.

throws on a function announces that it can fail. try marks the possibly failing operation. do groups operations whose errors you want to handle, and catch runs when one throws. Return a clear result in both success and failure paths. A LoadResult can contain an entries array and a message. On damaged input, returning an empty collection plus a message containing could not be read makes recovery visible without crashing. Do not use try! for this case: it assumes success and would turn a decoding failure into a crash. A controlled fallback should not silently overwrite the damaged file before a real app's recovery policy is decided.

options: .atomic asks Data to write through an auxiliary file and replace the destination on success, reducing the risk of exposing a partly written destination. Atomic means one indivisible update at that file-replacement level; it does not turn several separate files or read-modify-write operations into a transaction. Two writers can still overwrite each other's changes without coordination. A consistency invariant is something that should stay true through valid operations. Moving three of twelve entries from planned to done should keep twelve total. A crash after deleting them but before inserting them elsewhere can violate that total if the change is split into unrelated writes.

For the exercise, use Codable PracticeEntry values, encode the supplied Swift/20 entry, save atomically at the supplied temporary file URL, and load it through the URL function. Return an empty collection and a could not be read message for the broken-byte fixture. The checks establish file round-tripping and controlled malformed-data recovery within one run. The companion removes its sandbox after runs, so this does not demonstrate survival across app restarts. In a real Xcode app, use an appropriate persistent application-support location and test stop/relaunch separately; old file formats may also need migrations, meaning deliberate conversion to a new format. AS a and AS b give the tables short names. The dot in a.id means the id column from table a. ON specifies the matching condition: a book belongs to an author when b.author_id equals a.id. Run this query on the same tables:
```sql
SELECT a.name AS author, b.title
FROM demo_authors AS a
LEFT JOIN demo_books AS b
  ON b.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY a.id, b.title;

You get Nora/Garden Gate, Nora/Sea Path, Luis/Sky Notes, and Imani/NULL. LEFT JOIN preserves each left-side author. When there is no matching book, right-side columns are NULL in the result. SQL has not stored an imaginary book for Imani.

FROM demo_authors AS a
LEFT JOIN demo_books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id;
```

title: Choose an activity
summary: Use a conditional to recommend an activity and handle an unknown choice.
explanation: Sometimes you choose among several named options instead of just true and false. switch examines one value and selects a matching case. A case names a supported value and the work for it. default handles values that are not listed in other cases. Swift requires a switch to cover every possible input. A String can contain countless different words, so a few named String cases normally need default. The fallback should be useful to a person; it is part of the planned behavior, rather than an accidental result.

This complete Swift program suggests materials for a few crafts.

```swift
func supplies(for craft: String) -> String {
    switch craft {
    case "drawing":
        return "Bring pencils and paper."
    case "knitting":
        return "Bring yarn and needles."
    case "origami":
        return "Bring square paper."
    default:
        return "Choose a craft for a supply suggestion."
    }
}
print(supplies(for: "drawing"))
print(supplies(for: "unknown"))
```

The first call gives the drawing suggestion. The second reaches default. The colon after each case separates its match from its instructions. Quotes mark text values, and braces hold the switch inside the function.

In func supplies(for craft: String), for is the argument label used by the caller, and craft is the parameter name used inside. The call says supplies(for: "drawing") so its purpose reads naturally. Inside, switch craft reads the supplied String. -> String promises a text result. Each case uses return to give that result and end the call. A Swift switch does not automatically run the following case after one matches. You do not need a break after these returns. Matching these Strings is exact, so "Drawing" differs from "drawing".

A fallback keeps unknown input understandable. Unknown may mean a typo, a newly added option, or simply a value the function does not support. Do not claim it was one of the supported cases. Return a message inviting a supported choice. This is also why a switch with a default can keep working when an unexpected value arrives. It does not mean your function understands every possible activity; it means it has an intentional response for the ones it does not understand.

This separate complete program introduces combined true-or-false conditions.

```swift
let isWarm = true
let hasFreeTime = false
let canGoOutside = isWarm && hasFreeTime
let canDoSomething = isWarm || hasFreeTime
let needsMoreTime = !hasFreeTime
print(canGoOutside)
print(canDoSomething)
print(needsMoreTime)
```

&& means AND: both sides must be true, so the first result is false. || means OR: at least one side must be true, so the second is true. ! means NOT: it flips true and false, so the third is true. These operators produce Bool values you can use in an if condition.

AND needs both requirements. If isSunny is true and hasTime is false, isSunny && hasTime is false because one needed part is missing. You can check it by saying both values aloud: “sunny, but no time.” For OR, the same inputs produce true because one option is enough. Conditions are not Strings: "true" is text while true is a Bool. A method such as message.contains("paper") also returns a Bool, which asks whether those exact letters appear in the String. That is the kind of content check this exercise uses.

```swift
let message = "Bring paper"
print(message.contains("paper"))
print(message.contains("yarn"))
```
This prints true, then false. contains receives the text to look for and returns a Bool; it does not change message.

For the activity function, accept a String through the label for and switch on that input. Handle hiking with a message containing trail, reading with book, and cycling with helmet. Give unlisted input a fallback containing Choose with that capital C. Tests inspect those message parts rather than forcing a single full sentence. Try all three supported values and an unknown one. Predict which case each call selects. Also explain why a default is necessary for a String switch with only a few named cases.

analogy.limit: The default case is only a fallback; it should not hide choices that deserve their own result.

title: Count down with a loop
summary: Use a loop to print 3, 2, and 1 once each, then print Done!.
explanation: A loop repeats a block of instructions. A for loop takes values from a sequence one at a time and runs the block for each. A finite sequence has a limited number of values, so this loop stops after visiting them all. You do not need to tell it to stop by closing the app. The loop's variable holds the current value during each turn. Code after the closing brace runs after the loop finishes. Put a completion message there if you want it printed once instead of after every number.

This is a complete countdown program with different practice numbers.

```swift
var countdown: [Int] = []
for number in (2...5).reversed() {
    countdown.append(number)
    print(number)
}
let finished = "Lift off!"
print(finished)
```

2...5 is a closed range containing 2, 3, 4, and 5. reversed() visits them in the opposite order: 5, 4, 3, 2. The output shows those numbers once each, then Lift off!. The array collects the same sequence so you can inspect it after the loop.

Three dots ... create a closed range that includes both endpoints. The half-open range operator ..< includes the start but excludes the end. 2..<5 therefore contains 2, 3, and 4. Parentheses around a range let you call a method on the whole range, such as (2...5).reversed(). A method is a function associated with a value. The parentheses after reversed are empty because this call takes no arguments. Choose your range carefully; an extra included endpoint can make a loop run one more time than expected.

An array is an ordered collection. [Int] means an array whose elements are whole numbers. [] is an empty array; the explicit type tells Swift what kind of items it will later hold. var lets the array change. append(number) adds the current loop value at the end. If the loop visits 5 then 4, the array begins [5, 4], not [4, 5]. print(number) displays that turn's value. Collecting data and printing data are different jobs; printed output does not automatically create an array.

This second complete example compares the two range kinds.

```swift
var closedValues: [Int] = []
for value in 4...6 {
    closedValues.append(value)
}
var openValues: [Int] = []
for value in 4..<6 {
    openValues.append(value)
}
print(closedValues)
print(openValues)
```

The arrays are [4, 5, 6] and [4, 5]. Each closing brace ends that loop's repeated block. The two print calls occur afterward and run once each. A closed whole-number range from 4 through 6 contains three values: count both endpoints, not just the difference between them.

A countdown subtracts one each step in this example. Starting at four gives 4, 3, 2, 1, so after 2 comes 1. Stopping at 1 differs from including 0. A Set is a collection of distinct values; duplicates are counted only once. Set(countdown).count compared with countdown.count can reveal whether the array repeats a value. That check does not prove the order, so another check compares the whole array. Knowing what each check can tell you helps explain why both order and uniqueness matter.

```swift
let repeated = [3, 2, 2]
let unique = Set(repeated)
print(unique.count)
print(repeated.count)
```
This prints 2, then 3. Set receives the sequence and creates a set with one member per distinct value; the original array remains unchanged. No order of the set is promised.

For this exercise, loop over (1...3).reversed() to visit 3, 2, 1. Append and print each number inside the loop. After it closes, set finished to exactly Done! and print it once. The checks expect the array in that order, no repeated numbers, and the completion text. They do not replace inspecting the output when the instructions ask for each print once. Predict how many loop turns occur and how many completion prints occur. If Done! appears three times, look for its print inside the repeated block.

analogy.limit: A loop only stops when its range ends or its condition becomes false.

explanation: A function is also a value in JavaScript. You can give it a name, pass it as an argument, and let another function call it. A function received this way is called a callback. A higher-order function is one that receives or returns a function. These names describe what the code does; there is no extra magic syntax needed to pass a callback.

Distinguish the function from its result. `friendly` means the function itself. `friendly("Noor")` calls it immediately and means the value it returns. If a receiving function expects something it can call, pass the function name without parentheses. Its parameter can then hold that function value and call it with an input.

Backticks make a template literal, a string that can insert values. Inside it, `${name}` evaluates name and adds its value to the text. The dollar sign and braces mark the insertion; ordinary quoted strings do not perform this insertion. Function parentheses contain inputs, function braces contain instructions, and template-literal braces surround an expression to insert. Their meaning comes from where they appear.

title: Tuples, Dictionaries, & Sets
summary: Use a tuple for coordinates, a dictionary for details, and a set for unique tags.
explanation: Different collections fit different jobs. A tuple holds ordered values that cannot be replaced through tuple indexes. A dictionary connects keys to values so you can look up details by name. A set keeps unique members without a meaningful position order. The right choice depends on whether you need a fixed sequence, named fields, or uniqueness.

A tuple often uses parentheses, such as `(7, 2)`, with commas between values. Its first position is index 0. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma, `(7,)`; parentheses alone around 7 do not make a tuple. You cannot assign a new value to point[0]. A tuple name can still be reassigned to a different tuple, and a nested mutable value can still change; the coordinate tuple here contains only numbers.

A dictionary uses braces with a colon between each key and value.
```python
point = (7, 2)
item = {"title": "Garden Log", "year": 2018}
print(point[0])
print(item["title"])
item["year"] = 2019
print(item["year"])
```
This prints 7, Garden Log, and 2019. Brackets with a number read a tuple position. Brackets with a string key read a dictionary field. Dictionary entries can be updated; changing the year does not replace the title.

A set also uses braces, but its entries do not have key/value colons. `{"nature", "art", "nature"}` keeps only one nature entry. `len(tags)` counts distinct members. Sets do not supply ordered indexes, so do not use tags[0]. An empty set is `set()` because empty braces `{}` create a dictionary. Choose a list when order and duplicates matter.

```python
tags = set(["nature", "art", "nature"])
print(len(tags))
print(len(set()))
```
This prints 2, then 0. set receives an iterable and returns its distinct values in a new set; with no argument it returns an empty set. The list input is not changed.

This complete example demonstrates uniqueness and shared members.
```python
tags = {"nature", "art", "nature"}
print(len(tags))
print("nature" in tags)
first = {"gold", "silver"}
second = {"silver", "copper"}
shared = first & second
print(len(shared))
print("silver" in shared)
```
It prints 2, True, 1, and True. The in comparison asks whether a member belongs to a collection. The ampersand `&` finds the intersection: members present in both sets. No output relies on which order a set happens to display.

The math question gives red and blue in one set and blue and green in the other. Blue is the only shared member, so the intersection size is 1. The same uniqueness idea removes a duplicate tag in your project. A tuple's ordered pair is useful for coordinates; a dictionary's keys are useful for title and year; a set's distinct membership is useful for tags.

Your supplied coordinates are (4, 9), the dictionary's title is Cloud Atlas, and repeated mystery tags should count once alongside travel. That gives two distinct tags. Read the title using its key and use len to check the set's size. Do not turn it into a list just to depend on a displayed order; uniqueness, not ordering, is the behavior this project needs.

title: A reaction timer
summary: Record a start timestamp when the signal is shown.
explanation: The program needs state: stored information that can change between actions. Use let for the saved start and elapsed values. `null` means there is no recorded value yet. Use null rather than 0 as the missing marker because zero can be a valid timestamp or duration. A signal saves a starting time; a later click can calculate the difference.

`!==` means strict inequality: are these values different? The guard allows calculation only when startedAt is different from null. An early click must be ignored because no signal time exists. `Math.max(a, b)` chooses the larger number. Taking the maximum of 0 and the difference prevents a negative duration when supplied times are out of order. It cannot turn a bad clock reading into a reliable measurement.

In a real browser button, a click event listener can call `clickAt(Date.now())` when clicked. The signal action would call `signal(Date.now())` at its starting moment. Pass a function to addEventListener so the browser can run it later. Your exercise tests the timing functions with fixed numbers instead, which makes the expected difference predictable and repeatable without waiting for a person's click.

The supplied round begins at 1000 and clicks at 1240, so elapsed is 240 milliseconds. For 500 and 650, it is 150 milliseconds. Check normal, early, and reset cases separately. Starting a new signal should clear the previous elapsed result; reset should clear the start too. A timing measurement from this simple clock is a practice estimate, and real applications may use a monotonic clock for durations that must ignore wall-clock adjustments.
